common_name: Cupid Bush Cherry (Romance Series Dwarf Sour Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container bushes in early spring once soil is workable, in full sun with good drainage; late bloom timing helps this selection dodge spring frosts that can nip other orchard cherries.

directions: Cupid is one of the University of Saskatchewan's Romance series dwarf sour cherries, bred from Mongolian cherry and sour cherry crosses to survive prairie winters that would kill standard tart cherry trees. It carries the largest fruit of the whole series, with glossy near-black cherries that lean sweeter than typical pie cherries, and its later bloom time helps it avoid late frost damage that can thin crops on earlier-flowering siblings. Grow as a self-fertile, multi-stemmed bush in full sun on well-drained soil, watering regularly while fruit sizes up but backing off once plants are established. Renewal-prune a few of the oldest stems out every few years to keep the bush productive and open.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring once frost danger has passed, in average well-drained soil; stake or trellis the arching canes if a tidier form is wanted.

directions: Crimson Star is a selected goji berry trade clone grown commercially in northwestern China and prized for producing noticeably larger, brighter red fruit than seed-grown wolfberry plants. It is self-fertile and often sets a light crop the year after planting, with purple flowers opening over a long summer season followed by waves of ripening berries. The upright, arching shrub is drought tolerant once rooted in and performs best in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil rather than rich garden loam. Cut back hard in late winter to control its sprawling habit and encourage new fruiting canes, and expect some root suckering that is easy to remove or use for propagation.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; mass several plants together since this low, spreading groundcover fills in by rhizomes rather than growing as a single bush.

directions: Fundy was selected in 1969 at Nova Scotia's Kentville Research Station from open-pollinated seedlings of the older 'Augusta' clone, chosen for its upright growth and large, attractive berries well suited to pick-your-own plantings. Unlike highbush types, it spreads into a low mat by underground rhizomes and is typically managed on a two-year burn-or-mow pruning cycle to renew fruiting wood, much like wild lowbush stands. Give it full sun and acidic, well-drained soil, and expect a light crop the year after a renewal cutback followed by a heavier crop the second year. It is extremely cold hardy and needs little input beyond periodic stand renewal and weed control while establishing.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; this vigorous selection spreads readily and fills a planting faster than most other named lowbush clones.

directions: Blomidon, selected in 1970 at Nova Scotia's Kentville Research Station from a controlled cross rather than a wild-stand selection, was the first named lowbush blueberry bred specifically through hybridization. It is notably vigorous and high yielding, spreading by rhizomes into a dense low mat of dark green foliage topped with white spring flowers and uniform, large fruit. Like other lowbush selections, it is managed on a rotational pruning cycle, with stems mowed or burned back every other year to stimulate the flowering wood that bears the following season's crop. Grow in full sun on acidic, well-drained soil and expect berries sized and flavored closer to highbush blueberries than typical wild lowbush fruit.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; combine with another named lowbush clone to extend the harvest window and improve pollination.

directions: Chignecto is a Kentville Research Station lowbush blueberry release named in the late 1970s, notable among the Nova Scotia named clones for carrying the highest anthocyanin content of the group along with consistently good fruit set. Like its sibling selections it spreads by underground rhizomes into a low, dense colony rather than forming an upright bush, and is managed on a biennial mow-or-burn cycle that sacrifices one season's crop to renew vigorous flowering wood. Plant in full sun on lean, acidic, well-drained soil and avoid richer garden loam, which favors foliage over fruit. Its deeply pigmented berries make it a good choice for growers or home gardeners interested in high-antioxidant fruit for processing as well as fresh eating.
